'''''Ludisia''''' ('''''Lus.'''''<ref>Alphabetical List of Standard Abbreviations for Natural and Hybrid Generic Names, Royal Horticultural Society, https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/plant-registration-forms/orchid-name-abbreviations-list.pdf</ref>) is a genus of orchids<ref>Sherif, N. A., Senthil Kumar, T., & Rao, M. V. (2020). DNA barcoding and genetic fidelity assessment of micropropagated Aenhenrya rotundifolia (Blatt.) C.S. Kumar and F.N. Rasm.: a critically endangered jewel orchid. Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants, 26(12), 2391–2405. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12298-020-00917-9
Huang, L. ‐W., Wang, C. ‐J., Lin, Y. ‐S., Chung, W. ‐C., & Chung, W. ‐H. (2014). Stem rot of jewel orchids caused by a new forma specialis, F usarium oxysporum f. sp. anoectochili in T aiwan. Plant Pathology, 63(3), 539–547. https://doi.org/10.1111/ppa.12133</ref> that was thought to contain just one species, '''''Ludisia discolor''''', commonly referred to as [[jewel orchid]].  A second species,  '''''Ludisia ravanii''''', from the [[Philippines]], was described in 2013.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77132555-1|title = Ludisia ravanii Cootes & G.Tiong | Plants of the World Online | Kew Science}}</ref> '''''Ludisia discolor'''''  is native to Southern [[China]], Northeast [[India]], [[Thailand]], [[Vietnam]], the [[Philippines]], [[Malaysia]], [[Indonesia]] and [[Myanmar]],<ref>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=115489 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref> and often cultivated.

== Description ==
They are terrestrial orchids that in their natural setting would be found growing on the forest floor. They are known for their foliage, which is often velvety deep maroon with red veins that run parallel to the centre of the leaf.

Flowers are white with twisting yellow [[column (botany)|columns]]. Individual flowers are small but grow in clusters on upright stalks. Flowers in cultivation last a month or more.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200028741 Flora of China v 25 p 55, 血叶兰 xue ye lan, ''Ludisia discolor'' (Ker Gawler) Blume, Coll. Orchid. 113. 1859. ]</ref>

== Cultivation ==
They need high humidity and warm temperatures with low to medium light, and they tolerate extremely low light levels.

=== Conservation ===
Like many species today, ''Ludisia discolor'' and other species of terrestrial orchids face threats due to climate change and other environmental factors. Studies today that aim to understand more about how orchid species could be cultivated include micropropagation. When micropropagating ''Ludisia discolor'' in varying environments, they found that the plant was able to adapt to the environment while maintaining 99% genetic similarity with the parent plant. Now that scientists are able to control the genetic diversity of a plant in varying conditions, it will be beneficial in improving the species’ population numbers.

Apart from climate change and similar environmental factors, the species is currently facing threats of ''Fusarium oxysporum'', which manifests as a stem rot, affecting the flowering of some species of orchids.<ref>Sherif, N. A., Senthil Kumar, T., & Rao, M. V. (2020). DNA barcoding and genetic fidelity assessment of micropropagated Aenhenrya rotundifolia (Blatt.) C.S. Kumar and F.N. Rasm.: a critically endangered jewel orchid. Physiology and Molecular Biology of Plants, 26(12), 2391–2405. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12298-020-00917-9</ref><ref>Huang, L. ‐W., Wang, C. ‐J., Lin, Y. ‐S., Chung, W. ‐C., & Chung, W. ‐H. (2014). Stem rot of jewel orchids caused by a new forma specialis, F usarium oxysporum f. sp. anoectochili in T aiwan. Plant Pathology, 63(3), 539–547. https://doi.org/10.1111/ppa.12133</ref>

=== Cultivars ===
''Ludisia discolor'' has two notable cultivars:{{citation needed|date=October 2013}}
* ''L. discolor'' 'Alba', an albino variant, and
* ''L. discolor'' 'Nigrescens', a mutation often referred to as "black velvet".

== Hybrids ==
Hybrids of ''Ludisia'' with other orchid genera are placed in the following nothogenera:
* ''[[Dossisia]]''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/horticulturaldatabase/orchidregister/orchiddetails.asp?ID=2833|title = The International Orchid Register / RHS Gardening}}</ref> (''Dsi.'') = ''Ludisia'' × ''[[Dossinia]]'' 
* ''[[Goodisia]]''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/horticulturaldatabase/orchidregister/orchiddetails.asp?ID=135758|title=The International Orchid Register / RHS Gardening}}</ref> (''Gda.'') = ''Ludisia'' × ''[[Goodyera]]''
* ''[[Ludochilus]]''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/horticulturaldatabase/orchidregister/orchiddetails.asp?ID=166415|title=The International Orchid Register / RHS Gardening}}</ref> (''Lud.'') = ''Ludisia'' × ''[[Anoectochilus]]''
* ''[[Macodisia]]''<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/horticulturaldatabase/orchidregister/orchiddetails.asp?ID=157988|title=The International Orchid Register / RHS Gardening}}</ref> (''Mcd.'') = ''Ludisia'' × ''[[Macodes]]''
Note that these hybrids are with other genera in the subtribe [[Goodyerinae]], all commonly referred to as ''jewel orchids''.

(The given references are to registered primary hybrids within each given nothogenus.)
